senses.def: caper (Capparis spinosa): the shrub and its flower buds, eaten pickled

examples.tr: Pickled caper buds are the “capers” of Western cooking.

funFacts: Arabic كَبَر (kabar), Greek κάππαρις (kápparis), German Kaper and English caper are all the same word.
pitfalls: 酸豆 alone often means tamarind (also 酸角) on the Mainland — say 刺山柑 to be clear.

profile.feeling: A spiky orange curiosity with green jelly inside.

senses.def: kiwano, horned melon (Cucumis metuliferus)

examples.text: 火参果外面是橙黄色的，长满了刺。
examples.tr: A kiwano is orange-yellow outside and covered in spikes.

examples.tr: Inside, a kiwano has green, jelly-like flesh.

funFacts: It is a cucumber relative (Cucumis): the jelly tastes like cucumber with a hint of banana and lime.
In the Kalahari the wild plant is a source of water.
pitfalls: 火参果 is not 人参果, which is the pepino melon (a nightshade).
参 is shēn here, as in 人参.
subtleties: Sold in China as an exotic fruit, although the plant is a cucumber relative.

senses.def: lima bean, butter bean (Phaseolus lunatus)

examples.text: 棉豆又大又扁，煮熟以后又软又糯。
examples.tr: Lima beans are big and flat, soft and creamy once cooked.

棉 mián (cotton) is not 绵 mián (soft, continuous).
subtleties: In Britain the dried white ones are called butter beans.

profile.feeling: Crinkly green winter cabbage of Central Europe.

senses.def: Savoy cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. sabauda)

examples.text: 皱叶甘蓝的叶子皱皱的，比普通卷心菜软。
examples.tr: Savoy cabbage has crinkly leaves, softer than ordinary cabbage.

etymology.text: 皱叶 (‘wrinkled leaves’) + 甘蓝 (‘cabbage, Brassica oleracea’): a descriptive name.

funFacts: English Savoy comes from the Savoy region in the Alps; German Wirsing comes from Italian (Lombard) verza.
pitfalls: In 甘蓝, 蓝 is an old plant word (as in the indigo plant), not the colour blue.
subtleties: Its looser, crinkled leaves cook faster than a smooth white cabbage.

examples.tr: The guar gum in ice cream is extracted from guar seeds.

funFacts: Most of the world’s guar is grown in India and Pakistan, much of it for guar gum, used in food and in oil drilling.
pitfalls: 瓜尔 is only a sound here; it has nothing to do with 瓜 ‘melon’.
subtleties: A Mainland name (Wiktionary); in Taiwan the bean is 关华豆.

profile.feeling: Comfort soups, sushi rolls, crispy snacks.

senses.def: laver, nori (Porphyra/Pyropia seaweeds), usually dried in sheets

examples.text: 紫菜蛋花汤又简单又好喝。
examples.tr: Laver and egg-drop soup is simple and tasty.

examples.tr: To make sushi you roll the rice up in a sheet of nori.

etymology.text: 紫 (‘purple’) + 菜 (‘vegetable’): fresh laver is purplish-red, turning dark green-black when dried and roasted.

funFacts: Welsh laverbread is made from the same kind of seaweed.
The British phycologist Kathleen Drew-Baker worked out the laver life cycle (1949), which saved Japan’s nori farming; she is honoured there as the “Mother of the Sea”.
pitfalls: In Eastern Min (Fuzhou), 紫菜 can mean eggplant (Wiktionary).
subtleties: 紫菜 is the seaweed in general, as in soups; 海苔 suggests the crisp roasted sheets or snacks.

funFacts: Cantonese 胜瓜 replaces 丝 because it sounds like 输 ‘lose’ — the same taboo that turned 猪舌 ‘pig’s tongue’ into 猪脷.
pitfalls: English ‘Chinese okra’ (Wiktionary’s gloss) means this gourd — not okra (秋葵).
subtleties: Old dried fruits turn fibrous, but the bath sponge is usually made from the smooth luffa (丝瓜).

pitfalls: Don’t mix up 四棱豆 (winged bean) and 四季豆 (green bean).
subtleties: Its ripe seeds are about as rich in protein as soybeans.

cowpea, black-eyed pea (Vigna unguiculata) and its dry beans

the precise name of the yardlong bean

pitfalls: Wiktionary’s gloss is ‘cowpea; black-eyed pea’ — the long green 豇豆 at a Chinese market is the yardlong bean, a cowpea subspecies.
豇 is jiāng (1st tone), like 江 ‘river’.
subtleties: What 豆角 means depends on the region: green beans (四季豆) in much of the north, long beans in many southern places.

Italian romanesco means ‘Roman’.

funFacts: 卡宴 is also how Chinese writes the Porsche Cayenne.
pitfalls: 宴 (banquet) is only a sound here.
subtleties: Around 30,000–50,000 Scoville units: hotter than a jalapeño (墨西哥辣椒), milder than a habanero (哈瓦那辣椒).

profile.feeling: Fruity, fiery little lanterns.

senses.def: habanero (Capsicum chinense): a small, lantern-shaped, very hot chili

examples.text: 哈瓦那辣椒非常辣，切的时候最好戴手套。
examples.tr: Habaneros are extremely hot — best wear gloves when you cut them.
examples.py: Hāwǎnà làjiāo fēicháng là, qiē de shíhou zuìhǎo dài shǒutào.

examples.text: 哈瓦那辣椒小小的，像个灯笼。
examples.tr: A habanero is small and shaped like a lantern.

etymology.text: 哈瓦那 (Havana, Spanish La Habana) + 辣椒 (‘chili’): like Spanish habanero, ‘from Havana’.

pitfalls: The name says Havana, but the pepper is grown mainly in Mexico’s Yucatán — not specially Cuban.
subtleties: About 100,000–350,000 Scoville units, with a fruity aroma behind the heat.

profile.feeling: Plump, sweet, snapping-crisp pods.

senses.def: sugar snap pea, snap pea: a pea with thick, edible pods

examples.text: 甜豆的豆荚比荷兰豆厚，里面的豆子也更饱满。
examples.tr: Sugar snaps have thicker pods than snow peas, and plumper peas inside.
examples.py: Tiándòu de dòujiá bǐ hélándòu hòu, lǐmian de dòuzi yě gèng bǎomǎn.

examples.text: 甜豆连荚一起吃，又甜又脆。
examples.tr: Sugar snaps are eaten pod and all — sweet and crisp.
examples.py: Tiándòu lián jiá yìqǐ chī, yòu tián yòu cuì.

examples.text: 甜豆焯一下水就可以凉拌。
examples.tr: Blanch sugar snaps briefly and they’re ready for a cold dish.
examples.py: Tiándòu chāo yíxià shuǐ jiù kěyǐ liángbàn.

synonyms.nuance: ‘sweet crisp bean’: the fuller name, used on labels and by Chinese Wikipedia

etymology.text: 甜 (‘sweet’) + 豆 (‘bean, pea’).

funFacts: Sugar snap peas were bred in the United States in the 1970s by crossing snow peas with garden peas.
pitfalls: 甜豆 is not 荷兰豆 (snow pea, flat) or 豌豆 (shelling pea) — though all three are peas.
subtleties: Pull off the string along the seam before cooking.

absent.reason: Moringa pods are not a common vegetable in China and have no word of their own; Wiktionary has none.
absent.use: The tree is 辣木 (moringa), known in China for its seeds (辣木籽) and leaf powder; the pods are described as 辣木的豆荚 ‘moringa pods’.

absent.reason: Ivy gourd is not a market vegetable in China; Wiktionary has no Chinese word for it (its 紅瓜 means other things in Min dialects).
absent.use: Botanical name 红瓜 (Coccinia grandis); otherwise the Indian name tindora.

absent.reason: Tomatillos are barely known in China; Wiktionary has no Chinese word.
absent.use: Botanical name 黏果酸浆 (‘sticky-fruited Physalis’) — a relative of the Chinese lantern 酸浆; otherwise described as 墨西哥的一种绿色果子 ‘a green Mexican fruit’.

absent.reason: Sea kale is a European coastal plant unknown in China; Wiktionary has no Chinese word.
absent.use: Described as 海甘蓝 ‘sea cabbage’ (a translation, the Wikidata label); botanically Crambe maritima.

absent.reason: Dulse is a North Atlantic red seaweed not eaten in China; neither Wiktionary nor Chinese Wikipedia has a Chinese name.
absent.use: Described as 一种红藻 ‘a red seaweed’ from Ireland and Iceland, or by its Latin name Palmaria palmata.

absent.reason: Armenian cucumber is unknown in Chinese markets; there is no established word.
absent.use: Translated as 亚美尼亚黄瓜 ‘Armenian cucumber’ — though botanically it is a melon (甜瓜).

absent.reason: Rapini (broccoli rabe) is hardly sold in China; there is no established everyday word and Wiktionary has none.
absent.use: Chinese Wikipedia files it as 西洋菜薹 (‘Western flowering-stem vegetable’); it is compared with its close relative 菜心 (choy sum).

absent.reason: Cucamelons are a novelty in China with no established name; Wiktionary has none.
absent.use: Sold online under descriptive names such as 拇指西瓜 ‘thumb watermelon’ — it looks like a tiny watermelon but tastes like cucumber.

absent.reason: Pointed gourd (parwal) is an Indian vegetable unknown in China; Wiktionary has no Chinese word.
absent.use: Described as 印度的一种瓜 ‘an Indian gourd’ of the Trichosanthes genus (栝楼属), or by its Hindi name parwal (परवल).

absent.reason: Padrón peppers are a Spanish speciality with no Chinese name.
absent.use: Described as 西班牙的一种小青椒 ‘a small Spanish green pepper’.

absent.reason: Acorn squash is rare in China and has no established word; Wiktionary has none.
absent.use: Translated as 橡子南瓜 ‘acorn pumpkin’ (the Wikidata label), or just 一种小南瓜 ‘a small squash’.
